question: According to the manual, an approved helmet should fit:
choice_c: Tightly at the base and loosely at the top
choice_d: Loosely at the base and tightly at the top
explanation: For the greatest safety, a helmet should fit snugly all the way around the head. A loose-fitting helmet is more likely to come off in a crash before it can protect the rider.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.3, 'Helmet Use'

question: A label from which organization gives added assurance of helmet quality beyond the required DOT standard?
explanation: A helmet should be designed to meet U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) and state standards; a label from the Snell Memorial Foundation gives added assurance of quality.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.3, 'Helmet Use'

question: Research cited in the manual found that helmeted riders, compared with unhelmeted riders, are how much more likely to survive a head injury in a crash?
explanation: No matter what the speed, helmeted riders are three times more likely to survive head injuries than those not wearing helmets at the time of the crash.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.3, 'Helmet Use'

question: At the speeds most crashes occur (under 30 mph), an approved helmet can reduce the number and severity of head injuries by about:
explanation: Most riders are riding slower than 30 mph when a crash occurs. At these speeds, helmets can reduce both the number and the severity of head injuries by 50%.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.3, 'Helmet Use'

question: The manual notes that most motorcycle crashes happen:
choice_b: On short trips, just a few minutes after starting out
explanation: Most crashes happen on short trips (less than five miles long), just a few minutes after starting out -- not on long trips.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.3, 'Helmet Use'

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the two primary types of helmets the manual describes?
choice_c: None of these -- both are listed
explanation: The manual describes two primary types of helmets, providing two different levels of coverage: three-quarter and full face. A half-shell open-face style is not one of the two listed.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.3, 'Helmet Selection'

question: A plastic faceshield offers an advantage over goggles because it:
choice_b: Is required by law while goggles are not
choice_c: Also protects the rest of the face, not just the eyes
choice_d: Works better at night when tinted
explanation: A plastic shatter-resistant faceshield can help protect the whole face in a crash, plus protect against wind, dust, dirt, rain, insects, and pebbles. Goggles protect the eyes but not the rest of the face.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.4, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: The manual states that a windshield:
choice_a: Is a substitute for a faceshield or goggles
choice_b: Is not a substitute for a faceshield or goggles
choice_c: Is required equipment on every motorcycle
choice_d: Eliminates the need for a helmet
explanation: A windshield is not a substitute for a faceshield or goggles -- most windshields will not protect a rider's eyes from the wind.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.4, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: Why does the manual caution against wearing eyeglasses or sunglasses alone as eye protection while riding?
choice_b: They fog up faster than a faceshield
choice_c: They reduce peripheral vision more than goggles
choice_d: They don't keep the eyes from watering and might blow off when the head is turned
explanation: Eyeglasses or sunglasses won't keep the rider's eyes from watering, and they might blow off when the rider turns their head while riding.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.4, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: When should tinted eye or face protection NOT be worn?
choice_b: At night or any other time when little light is available
explanation: Tinted eye protection should not be worn at night or any other time when little light is available, since it further reduces visibility.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.4, 'Eye and Face Protection'

question: Why does the manual recommend wearing a jacket even in warm weather?
choice_a: It is required by state law year-round
choice_c: Many jackets are designed to protect without overheating the rider, and help prevent dehydration
choice_d: It is the only garment that meets DOT standards
explanation: Wear a jacket even in warm weather to prevent dehydration; many are designed to protect without getting the rider overheated, even on summer days.

question: According to the manual, boots or shoes worn while riding should:
choice_a: Be high and sturdy enough to cover and support the ankles, with hard, slip-resistant soles
choice_b: Have long, loose laces for quick removal
choice_c: Be as lightweight and flexible as possible
choice_d: Have smooth soles for easy foot movement on the pegs
explanation: Boots or shoes should be high and sturdy enough to cover the ankles and give them support, with soles of hard, durable, slip-resistant material, short heels, and laces tucked in so they won't catch.

question: What must a rider wear whenever riding on a Class M learner's permit, according to the manual?
choice_b: Only a helmet, if riding after dark
choice_d: Nothing beyond what a licensed rider wears
explanation: All applicants with a permit must wear a helmet and eye protection, per the manual's introductory safe-rider checklist and the Earning Your License section.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.3 and p.39, 'Wear the Right Gear' / 'Earning Your License'
